blocks.text: Every message that flows between an MCP client and an MCP server has to be written down in some agreed shape, otherwise one side would send something the other side cannot parse. 0.

This lesson opens the Communication Protocol module by looking at exactly what JSON-RPC is, why MCP's designers picked it instead of rolling their own format, and the basic envelope shape you will see in every single message from here on.
1. What JSON-RPC Actually Is

blocks.alt: A client sends a JSON-RPC envelope to the server
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439737519-283314204.png

JSON-RPC is a tiny specification, short enough to read in ten minutes, that describes how to call a remote procedure, a function living on another machine or process, using plain JSON as the message format. RPC stands for remote procedure call, the general idea of asking some other program to run a function for you and hand back the result, as if it were a local function call even though it might be crossing a network or a process boundary.

The specification does not care what transport carries the bytes, it does not know or care whether the JSON travels over standard input and output pipes, a raw TCP socket, an HTTP POST body, or a WebSocket frame.
It only defines the shape of the JSON itself, the fields a request must have, the fields a response must have, and the rules for matching one to the other.

That separation of concerns, wire format on one side, transport on the other, is exactly why MCP layers cleanly on top of it, and it is also why the Transport Mechanisms module later in this curriculum can swap stdio for HTTP or Server-Sent Events without touching the message format at all.
2. Why MCP's Designers Chose JSON-RPC
2.1 A Note on Adoption

JSON-RPC was not created for MCP, it dates back to the mid 2000s as a lightweight alternative to heavier remote procedure call systems of that era. The Language Server Protocol adopted it around 2016 to standardize how editors talk to language tooling, and by the time MCP's designers were choosing a wire format, JSON-RPC already had years of production use, mature libraries in most languages, and a track record of being simple enough that teams rarely got it wrong.

MCP needed a message format that client and server libraries in many different programming languages could parse without a specialized library, since MCP servers and clients get written in Python, TypeScript, Java, Rust, and more. JSON parsing is built into essentially every mainstream language's standard library or is a one-line dependency, so choosing JSON as the base format meant nobody had to write a custom binary parser just to speak MCP.

JSON-RPC specifically, rather than plain ad hoc JSON, gave MCP a small set of rules that were already battle tested by other systems, most notably the Language Server Protocol that powers autocomplete and error checking in editors like VS Code.

Reusing a proven, minimal specification meant MCP's authors did not need to design request and response semantics from scratch, and any engineer who had already worked with JSON-RPC in another context could pick up MCP messages immediately.

items: Lightweight, a JSON-RPC envelope adds only a handful of required fields on top of your actual data.
Language agnostic, every mainstream language can produce and consume JSON with zero special tooling.
Transport agnostic, the same message shape works whether the bytes travel over stdio, HTTP, or a WebSocket.
Already proven, JSON-RPC 2.0 predates MCP by many years and has been exercised at scale by other protocols.

blocks.text: 3. The Three Message Kinds

blocks.alt: Request, response, and notification are the three message kinds
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439737520-608659303.png
3.1 Why a Third Kind Is Necessary

It might seem like requests and responses alone should cover everything, but plenty of real situations do not fit that shape. A server that wants to tell a client a resource just changed on disk has no question to ask and expects no answer back, forcing that announcement into a request-response pair would mean inventing a pointless reply just to satisfy the format.

Notifications solve exactly this by dropping the id field, which simultaneously tells the receiver two things, do not expect a reply to be waited for, and there is no reply to send back even if you wanted to. This keeps one-way announcements just as cheap and simple as two-way calls.

JSON-RPC defines exactly three kinds of message, and every single thing that crosses an MCP connection is one of these three. A request asks the other side to do something and expects a response back. A response answers a specific earlier request, carrying either a successful result or an error. A notification looks almost like a request but carries no id field, which signals that the sender does not want and will not wait for a reply.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Message kind","Has an id","Expects a reply"],"rows":[["Request","yes","yes"],["Response","yes, matches the request","n/a, it is the reply"],["Notification","no","no"]]}

blocks.text: Later lessons in this module go deep on each of these three individually, Request Messages and Response Messages are next, then Notifications gets its own full lesson. For now, the important thing is simply that these three shapes exhaust the possibilities, there is no fourth kind of JSON-RPC message hiding anywhere in MCP.
4. The Envelope Fields

blocks.alt: jsonrpc, id, method, and params make up the envelope
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439737520-94172692.png
4.1 Field Order and Extra Fields

JSON objects are unordered by definition, so nothing in JSON-RPC cares whether jsonrpc appears before or after id in the raw text, a parser reads field names, not field positions. Most real implementations put jsonrpc first purely as a human-readability convention, not because the specification requires it.

The specification also does not forbid extra fields beyond the ones it defines, though well-behaved MCP implementations avoid adding custom top-level fields to the envelope itself, preferring to put anything extra inside params, result, or the error object's data field instead, so the core envelope stays predictable across every implementation.

Every JSON-RPC message, whichever of the three kinds it is, starts with a jsonrpc field carrying the exact string 2.0. That field is a version marker, it tells the receiving side which revision of the specification the sender is following, and every MCP implementation should reject a message whose jsonrpc field is missing or wrong.

Beyond that shared jsonrpc field, a request adds method, the name of the operation being invoked, an optional params object carrying arguments, and an id used to match the eventual response. A response instead carries the same id, plus either a result field on success or an error field on failure, never both at once.
5. A Minimal Request and Response Pair

blocks.alt: A request pairs with a response
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439737520-737342864.png

A single connection is rarely limited to one request at a time. A client might send several tools/call and resources/read requests back to back without waiting for each response before sending the next, this is called pipelining, and it is exactly why the id field earns its own dedicated lesson later in this module.

Here is the smallest complete round trip you will see in MCP, a client asking a server to list its available tools, and the server answering. Notice the id, 7 in this example, appears identically in both messages, that shared value is what lets the client know which of possibly several in-flight requests this particular response belongs to.

Nothing about this pair mentions files on disk, sockets, or HTTP headers, that is deliberate, JSON-RPC only defines the content of the envelope, not how it physically moves. The Transport Mechanisms module covers the physical movement, this module stays entirely focused on what is written inside the envelope.
6. Why Not Just Use Plain REST or a Custom Format
6.1 A Third Alternative Considered: gRPC

gRPC, built on protocol buffers, is another popular remote procedure call system, and it is faster and more strongly typed than JSON-RPC in many benchmarks. It requires a compiled schema and generated code for every language a client or server is written in, which adds a build step that JSON-RPC simply does not need.

For MCP, whose entire value proposition rests on being easy for any tool author in any language to adopt with minimal setup, a plain text, schema-optional format that any JSON parser already understands won out over a faster but heavier binary alternative.
REST leans on HTTP verbs and URLs to express what operation is happening, a GET to one URL means something different from a POST to another.
That works well for resource-oriented APIs, but MCP needed something that felt equally natural over stdio, where there is no concept of a URL or an HTTP verb at all, just a stream of bytes.
JSON-RPC solves this by putting the operation name directly inside the message body, as the method field, so the same message shape works identically whether it travels over a pipe or a socket.

A fully custom format was also on the table early on, but it would have meant MCP's authors had to define every edge case themselves, how errors look, how requests and responses pair up, whether batching is allowed, and so on. JSON-RPC already answers all of those questions in a specification a few pages long, which let MCP's designers spend their design effort on the actual protocol semantics, tools, resources, prompts, rather than reinventing plumbing that already existed.
7. Where JSON-RPC Ends and MCP Begins

A quick preview of the vocabulary MCP builds on top of the bare envelope, these are the method names you will meet throughout the rest of this curriculum, each one just a string sitting inside an otherwise ordinary JSON-RPC request.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Method name","What it asks the server to do"],"rows":[["initialize","Begin the session and exchange capabilities"],["tools/list","Return the tools this server offers"],["tools/call","Actually invoke one named tool"],["resources/read","Fetch the contents of one resource"],["prompts/get","Fetch one named prompt template"]]}

blocks.text: It helps to draw a clean line here, JSON-RPC only defines the envelope, the jsonrpc field, the id, the method and params, the result and error. It has no opinion at all about what method names should exist or what params they should expect, that is entirely up to whatever protocol is built on top of it.

MCP is the layer that fills in those blanks, it defines specific method names like tools/list, tools/call, resources/read, and prompts/get, and it defines exactly what params each of those expects and what result shape comes back. Every MCP-specific concept you have learned so far in this curriculum, tools, resources, prompts, capabilities, ultimately gets expressed as JSON-RPC method names and params, wrapped inside the envelope this lesson describes.

blocks.title: A useful mental model
blocks.content: Think of JSON-RPC as the envelope and postage system, and MCP as the actual letter format and vocabulary written inside. The postal service does not care what language the letter is written in, it only cares that the envelope has a valid address and a stamp.

blocks.text: 8. Requests Versus Notifications, a Quick Preview

Because the id field is what separates a request from a notification, a server or client can tell instantly, just by checking whether id is present, whether it owes a reply. This distinction matters constantly in MCP, an initialize call is a request because the client genuinely needs the server's capabilities back before continuing, but a resource-changed announcement is a notification because the server does not need or want an acknowledgment.

The Notifications lesson later in this module explores this in much more depth, including exactly which situations call for a notification instead of a request, but it is worth seeing the contrast early, since it is the single most consequential structural choice a JSON-RPC message can carry.
9. Errors Are Part of the Same Envelope

blocks.alt: An error response uses the same JSON-RPC envelope
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439737521-827616985.png
9.1 The Optional data Field

Beyond code and message, an error object may include a data field carrying whatever extra detail the server thinks would help diagnose the problem, a stack trace, the specific argument that failed validation, or a suggested fix. Nothing about data's shape is fixed, unlike code and message it is intentionally open-ended.

When something goes wrong, JSON-RPC does not throw the connection away or send back some ad hoc string, it replies with a response whose error field replaces result. That error field itself has a fixed shape, a numeric code, a short human-readable message, and an optional data field for extra detail.

The Error Responses lesson later in this module walks through the standard codes and what a well-behaved client should do with each one. For now, just note that success and failure share the exact same envelope shape, jsonrpc and id are always present, and only the third field differs, result for success, error for failure.
10. IDs, Uniqueness, and Matching

blocks.alt: A request with an id gets a response with the same id
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439737521-7894567.png

The specification allows either a number or a string for id, MCP implementations commonly use small sequential integers, 1, 2, 3, but a UUID string works exactly as well as long as it stays unique among currently outstanding requests on that connection.

The id field deserves a lesson of its own later in this module, Message IDs, but the short version belongs here too, since it is such a core part of the envelope. An id can be a number or a string, it must be unique among the requests currently awaiting a reply on that connection, and whichever side sent the request is the one that chose the id, the responder simply echoes it back unchanged.

This matters because JSON-RPC connections are not strictly one request, then one response, then the next request. A client can fire off several requests before any responses come back, and the id field is the only thing that lets it later figure out which response answers which question.
11. Batching, a Brief Mention

blocks.title: Not every server supports batching
blocks.content: Batching is technically allowed by the JSON-RPC specification, but MCP servers are not required to support it, and some deliberately do not, since it complicates error handling. Always check a server's declared capabilities before relying on it.

blocks.text: The JSON-RPC specification also allows bundling several requests into a single array and sending them as one batch, with the server replying with a matching array of responses. This is useful when a client already knows it needs several independent operations and wants to save a network round trip by sending them all at once.

Batching gets its own full lesson later in this module, since there are real tradeoffs around when it helps and when it adds more complexity than it saves. For now it is enough to know that the envelope shape scales naturally from a single message to an array of them.
12. Streaming Results Are Layered On Top, Not Baked In

It is worth sitting with that idea for a moment, streaming in MCP is not a new envelope type, it is a pattern built entirely out of the request, response, and notification shapes this lesson already covered. Once those three shapes feel natural, streaming will feel like a natural consequence rather than a new concept to memorize.

JSON-RPC itself has no native concept of a response arriving in pieces, a response is a single complete JSON object. MCP achieves the feeling of a streaming result by sending a series of notifications carrying partial progress while the actual request is still pending, followed eventually by one final response that completes the original request.

This is a clever reuse of the existing envelope shapes rather than an extension to JSON-RPC itself, and the Streaming lesson later in this module walks through exactly how that pattern is built out of ordinary requests and notifications you already understand from this lesson.
13. Version Discipline, Why the jsonrpc Field Never Changes
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439737521-775105487.png
13.1 A Quick Word on Version Mismatches

If a client and server disagree on the MCP protocol version during initialize, that disagreement is resolved entirely through ordinary request and response fields, typically the server responding with whichever version it does support, never by changing the jsonrpc field itself. The Protocol Versioning lesson that closes this module covers the full negotiation process.

You might expect the jsonrpc field to change over time as MCP itself evolves, but it does not, it stays 2.0 forever, since it identifies the JSON-RPC specification version, not the MCP protocol version. MCP has its own, separate version negotiation, covered in the Protocol Versioning lesson that closes this module, and the two version numbers are entirely independent of each other.

Keeping these two concerns separate is a deliberate design choice, it means MCP can introduce new methods, new params shapes, or new capabilities across its own version history without ever needing to touch the underlying JSON-RPC envelope that every message is wrapped in.
14. Reading Your First Real MCP Trace

Here is the same style of trace, but this time the tool call fails partway through, notice that the shape of the failing response is still a completely ordinary JSON-RPC envelope, just with error instead of result.

If you turn on verbose logging in most MCP client libraries, what you will actually see scrolling past is a sequence of these JSON-RPC envelopes, one per line or one per log entry. Learning to read them quickly, spotting the id, checking whether it is a request, response, or notification, and reading the method or result or error, is the single most useful skill this module builds toward.

Arrows like these, one pointing out for messages the client sends and one pointing in for messages the server sends back, are a common convention in MCP debugging output and in this curriculum's own examples, worth getting comfortable with early.
Worked Example: Tracing a Single Tool Call by Hand
Now imagine that same get_current_time call fails because an invalid timezone was supplied, the response keeps the exact same id, 4, but swaps result for error entirely.
Suppose an AI assistant needs to call a get_current_time tool on a connected MCP server. Walk through what actually crosses the wire, starting from the moment the model decides to call the tool.

Every field in both messages should now be recognizable, jsonrpc marks the specification version, id 4 links the two together, method names the operation, params carries the tool name and its arguments, and result carries back whatever the tool produced. Nothing here is MCP magic, it is the envelope from this lesson, filled in with a tools/call method that the next lesson, Request Messages, explores in full depth.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting the jsonrpc field entirely, or sending the wrong version string, which many strict server implementations will reject outright.
Assuming JSON-RPC defines what methods exist, it does not, method names and their params and result shapes are entirely defined by MCP, not by JSON-RPC itself.
Treating a notification as if it needs a reply, or waiting on a response that will never arrive because no id was sent.
Confusing the JSON-RPC version, always 2.0, with the MCP protocol version, which is a completely separate field negotiated during initialize.
Mixing up result and error, a response should carry exactly one of the two, never both, and never neither.
Hand-rolling JSON parsing logic instead of using a language's standard JSON library, which usually leads to subtle bugs around escaping and number formatting.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Hint
blocks.content: Resources use a uri field inside params rather than name and arguments, check the resources/read example earlier in this lesson if you get stuck on the shape.

blocks.text: Take the tools/list request and response pair from earlier in this lesson and rewrite it as if it were, instead, a resources/list call returning two resources of your choosing. Keep the jsonrpc field, choose your own id, and make sure your response's id matches your request's id exactly.

Once you have written both messages, check them against the rules from this lesson, is jsonrpc exactly 2.0 in both, does the id match, does the response carry exactly one of result or error, and not both.
Key Takeaway

0 is the small, transport agnostic wire format MCP builds every single message on top of, giving client and server a shared envelope, jsonrpc, id, and either method plus params for a request or result plus error for a response, without either side needing to invent or agree on a custom format from scratch.
MCP itself then fills that envelope with its own vocabulary of method names and params shapes, tools/call, resources/read, and the rest, which is exactly what the rest of this module explores.

The next lesson, Request Messages, zooms in on one of the three message kinds introduced here and goes deep on how a request is actually built, the conventions behind method names like tools/call and tools/list, how params gets structured, and exactly what role the id field plays when a client has more than one request in flight at once.
